svg.text: Potassium: the narrowest window in the body
Normal 3.5 to 5.0 mmol/L. Both ends stop the heart.
LOW — under 3.5
SAFE — 3.5 to 5.0
HIGH — over 5.0
Too low
Causes: vomiting, diarrhoea, water tablets,
poor intake, insulin, salbutamol
Signs: weak floppy muscles, cramps, ileus,
palpitations, flattened T wave with a U wave
The lethal pairing: low potassium plus digoxin.
Low K makes a normal digoxin dose toxic.
Check magnesium too: potassium will not correct
while magnesium is low
Too high
Causes: kidney failure, crush injury, burns,
acidosis, stored blood, some BP tablets
Signs: often none until the arrest
ECG first: tall peaked T waves, then a wide
QRS, then a sine wave, then asystole
Order of treatment: calcium to protect the heart,
then insulin with glucose to move it into cells,
then something to remove it from the body
The rule that kills patients when it is broken
Concentrated potassium is NEVER given as a rapid push or a bolus. It causes cardiac arrest.
It is always diluted, always infused slowly, and peripherally not faster than about 10 mmol per hour
Faster rates need a central line, cardiac monitoring and a high dependency setting
Check the urine output first: giving potassium to a patient who is not passing urine is how it accumulates
